section: What the evidence establishes
text: Cambodia’s surface water and groundwater form a connected seasonal system. Rainfall, river stage, floodplain inundation, sediment layers and pumping determine when water enters storage and when it returns to rivers or is withdrawn. Groundwater can support dry-season supply, but a productive well does not by itself establish a renewable or chemically suitable resource. [S01, S04, S05, S06]

section: What the evidence establishes
text: The strongest practical conclusion is to manage quantity and quality together. Pumping decisions need aquifer tests and seasonal observations; drinking-water decisions need laboratory results and a reliable supply-management system. Published maps help locate questions and design investigations, while individual wells require their own evidence. [S04, S06, S08, S10]

section: What the evidence establishes
text: This article is a documentary research synthesis, not a new field survey, a national groundwater inventory or a real-time hydrological assessment. The evidence spans historical reports from 1957 and 1977 to a regional groundwater review published in 2026. Different dates, methods and geographic scales are retained throughout.

section: Cambodia within the Lower Mekong Basin
text: The Lower Mekong Basin and the Greater Mekong Region describe different areas. The basin is a drainage system shared by parts of Lao PDR, Thailand, Cambodia and Viet Nam, with upstream inflow from the Lancang–Mekong. The Greater Mekong groundwater review also covers aquifers outside that drainage basin, including systems in Myanmar and other parts of Thailand and Viet Nam. A regional aquifer map must therefore not be relabelled as a Lower Mekong catchment map. [S06, S11]

section: Cambodia within the Lower Mekong Basin
text: Cambodia receives the Mekong from the north, including contributions from the Sekong, Sesan and Srepok tributary system. Around Phnom Penh, the Mekong, Bassac and Tonle Sap River connect the upstream river corridor, the Great Lake and the downstream delta. Below Kratie, broad floodplains become central to seasonal storage and exchange. [S01, S02]

section: Cambodia within the Lower Mekong Basin
text: The Tonle Sap catchment and the Cambodian upper delta are the main lowland focus here. Northwestern and northeastern aquifers are included where they clarify Cambodian water supply. Coastal salinity and Kampot karst provide comparisons, but coastal catchments draining directly to the Gulf of Thailand are not automatically part of the Lower Mekong Basin. [S01, S06, S15]

section: The flood pulse and the Tonle Sap connection
text: During rising Mekong stages, the hydraulic gradient can drive water along the Tonle Sap River toward the lake, expanding seasonal inundation. As river levels fall, lake water drains toward the Mekong. Floodplains store water, receive sediment and provide habitats linked to fisheries and farming; damaging floods and beneficial seasonal inundation are related but different management concerns. [S01, S02]

section: The flood pulse and the Tonle Sap connection
text: The 2005 basin overview and 2009 flow booklet provide historical explanations of this system. They should not be read as descriptions of unchanged present-day flow. The 2023 State of the Basin Report documents a redistribution toward higher dry-season and lower flood-season flows in recent decades, reduced Tonle Sap reverse flow, and a later or shorter flood season. The report attributes changes to interacting development pressures and climatic conditions; this synthesis does not assign a percentage of change to any individual dam. [S03]

section: The flood pulse and the Tonle Sap connection
text: For Cambodia, management should consider the timing, duration and connectivity of inundation as well as annual water volume. A similar annual total can accompany a different seasonal pattern. River observations and lake levels are therefore useful alongside rainfall, water-use records and floodplain mapping. This is a monitoring implication drawn from the documented seasonal system, not an additional measured trend. [S01, S02, S03]

section: Where groundwater is stored
text: In lowland Cambodia, sand and gravel layers within alluvial deposits commonly form aquifers, while finer clay-rich layers impede vertical movement. The 2026 review describes both younger and older alluvium in the Tonle Sap plain and a layered Cambodian delta system. These categories are useful regional descriptors; they do not establish identical thickness, confinement or water quality everywhere. [S06, S07]

section: Where groundwater is stored
text: Younger floodplain deposits may contain local productive sand lenses within otherwise clay-rich material. Older alluvium can be an important source beneath or around the lowland margins. Bedrock aquifers in sandstone, basalt, weathered crystalline rocks and karst have different storage and flow behaviour. Their yields depend on connected fractures, weathering, sediment texture and well construction, rather than rock name alone. [S04, S06, S07, S15]

section: Where groundwater is stored
text: The USGS report and its plates provide a valuable historical map and cross-section baseline. They preserve well locations, lithology and the interpretation available at the time. Old province names, boundaries, settlement positions and drilling records need reconciliation with modern references before operational use. The plates are not a current drilling-success or drinking-water-safety map. [S07]

section: How rivers and aquifers exchange water
text: A gaining river receives groundwater where groundwater head exceeds river stage. A losing river supplies an aquifer where the river is higher and the bed allows exchange. The direction can reverse seasonally, and river-connected storage may be partly returned during recession. Clay layers, riverbed sediments and the distance from the channel affect the size and timing of that response. [S05]

section: How rivers and aquifers exchange water
text: Raksmey, Jinno and Tsutsumi’s 2009 study coupled groundwater-flow and recharge models for central and southern Cambodia. In the simulated 2002 conditions, the downstream Mekong and Bassac could gain groundwater during the dry season and lose water toward aquifers during the wet season. Other modelled reaches received groundwater from upland margins. These are results for particular model reaches and assumptions, not a rule that every Tonle Sap bank behaves identically. [S05]

section: How rivers and aquifers exchange water
text: A seasonal rise in well level is evidence of changing hydraulic conditions, but it does not alone quantify recharge or identify the source of the water. Useful tests combine paired river-stage and well-head measurements, screened-depth information, groundwater chemistry and, where justified, environmental tracers. Pumping can change gradients and capture water that would otherwise discharge to a river. These are investigation priorities consistent with the interaction model and recharge assessment. [S04, S05]

section: Recharge potential and the limits of regional maps
text: Lacombe and colleagues developed a Lower Mekong recharge model using baseflow estimates from 65 unregulated sub-catchments. The historical streamflow records fall within 1951–2007. Rainfall and evapotranspiration explain much of the spatial pattern at this scale; the prediction is mapped on a 0.25° grid. This resolution is appropriate for regional screening, not the design of an individual village well field. [S04, pp. 4–10]

section: Recharge potential and the limits of regional maps
text: The Cambodian comparisons in the paper are especially important. A northwestern sandstone study reported 10–70 mm/year, whereas the regional model indicated about 200 mm/year in that area. For a southeastern Cambodian case, a local groundwater model used about 20 mm/year, compared with about 230 mm/year in the regional assessment. Clay-rich cover and sparse local gauging are among the explanations discussed. These figures describe different methods and study footprints and must not be averaged into a single national rate. [S04, pp. 13–14]

section: Recharge potential and the limits of regional maps
text: Recharge is also different from a permissible pumping volume. A recharge estimate does not allocate the full amount to extraction: groundwater discharge supports rivers, wetlands and existing users, while changes in storage and lateral flow also matter. The water balance must be assessed over a suitable area and period, with drought and recovery included. No national safe yield or new extraction limit is calculated here. [S04, S09]

section: Arsenic, mineral reactions and other quality concerns
text: Arsenic is a major concern in parts of Cambodia’s young alluvial groundwater system. Cambodian field research demonstrates that arsenic can be released from near-surface, river-derived wetland sediments and transported through an aquifer. Redox conditions and groundwater flow both influence the resulting distribution. A district-level risk map cannot certify one household well. [S08]

section: Arsenic, mineral reactions and other quality concerns
text: The process connects hydrogeology with mineralogy: iron-bearing sediment phases can retain arsenic, while changes in reducing conditions and water–sediment interaction can release it. Iron staining or clear-looking water is not an arsenic test. The regional review treats arsenic, salinity and depletion as major development constraints; their overlap differs across aquifer units. [S06, S08]

section: Arsenic, mineral reactions and other quality concerns
text: WHO gives a provisional arsenic guideline value of 10 µg/L for drinking water. It is a health-based reference used here, not a statement of Cambodia’s current legal standard. Source selection and treatment need verified arsenic results and microbial safety; removing one chemical hazard does not establish that the water is safe overall. [S10]

section: Arsenic, mineral reactions and other quality concerns
text: Salinity may reflect coastal intrusion, older saline pore water, mineral dissolution or mixing; a high electrical-conductivity reading alone does not identify its source. The 2026 review distinguishes mapped observations from areas considered at risk. Salinity concerns reported for the wider Mekong Delta should not be transferred wholesale to every Cambodian floodplain aquifer. [S06]

section: Arsenic, mineral reactions and other quality concerns
text: The supplied 2018 field workbook and earlier hydrogeology page provide useful survey context, but field pH, conductivity and dissolved oxygen cannot substitute for laboratory arsenic, iron, manganese or microbiological results. Conductivity units in the supporting materials need reconciliation before conversion or threshold comparisons. This article does not publish unverified site contamination labels or reuse the earlier page’s summary statistics as new results. [S13, S14]

section: Groundwater use, dry-season irrigation and competing demands
text: Groundwater offers practical advantages where surface water is seasonally scarce or difficult to distribute. Its availability can support domestic supply and supplementary irrigation, but local development also changes drawdown, pumping costs and hydraulic connections. The appropriate scale of assessment is the aquifer system and its users, not just one successful borehole. [S04, S06]

section: Groundwater use, dry-season irrigation and competing demands
text: Erban and Gorelick’s 2016 modelling study identifies risks to shallow domestic water access from expansion of groundwater irrigation in Cambodia and discusses transboundary implications. Its projection horizon is tied to that study’s scenario and baseline. The reported “within 15 years” result must not be republished as a new countdown beginning in 2026 or as proof that depletion has already occurred everywhere. [S09]

section: Groundwater use, dry-season irrigation and competing demands
text: A practical response is conjunctive assessment: compare seasonal surface-water supply, groundwater storage, demand, water quality and the cost of reliable delivery. Establish pumping inventories and monitor recovery after the irrigation season. Proposed expansions should assess effects on nearby domestic wells and river or wetland discharge before treating groundwater as an unlimited drought reserve. These are research and management recommendations, not validated allocation rules. [S04, S06, S09]

section: Research priorities across Cambodia
text: Cambodia requires several complementary study settings rather than one uniform groundwater programme. The following priorities are an editorial synthesis of the reviewed evidence. They are study areas, not new protected areas, aquifer boundaries or claims of measured pollution. [S04, S05, S06, S15]

section: A focused surface-water and groundwater research programme
text: First, assemble the existing evidence: borehole logs, screen depths, pumping tests, abstraction estimates, river and lake gauges, rainfall records, floodplain elevations and water chemistry. Store dates, coordinates, vertical datums and units with each observation. River stage and groundwater head can be compared only after their reference elevations are reconciled. This is a proposed evidence-management workflow. [S04, S05, S06]

section: A focused surface-water and groundwater research programme
text: Second, monitor seasonal exchange along selected river-to-floodplain transects. Pair water-level records with field conductivity and temperature, and collect laboratory samples appropriate to the intended water use. Repeat observations across rising water, peak inundation, recession and the late dry season. Keep raw records separate from corrected values, document gaps and do not interpolate a missing season into an apparent measured trend.

section: A focused surface-water and groundwater research programme
text: Third, test site-scale recharge and pumping responses. Combine aquifer tests, water-level recovery, local stratigraphy and water balances. Where groundwater-source attribution changes a decision, use suitable geochemical or isotope methods with a clear sampling design. Evaluate uncertainty before using a regional recharge product to support a local irrigation proposal. [S04, S05]

section: A focused surface-water and groundwater research programme
text: Finally, connect the Cambodian upper delta evidence with Viet Nam through compatible hydrostratigraphic descriptions and monitoring practices. A 2026 governance study provides a framework for the shared Cambodia–Mekong River Delta aquifer system; only its abstract and metadata were checked here, so this article does not reproduce its scores or claim that its recommendations have been implemented. [S17]

section: Reading the maps and the evidence responsibly
text: The public figure gallery uses original USGS plates and source pages from the CC BY recharge paper. Whole-page reproductions retain the published legends and captions; the figures are not newly georeferenced GIS layers. Each caption states the source date and geographic scope. Open the source PDF for full detail.

section: Reading the maps and the evidence responsibly
text: The 2026 aquifer map is available from its original Zenodo record. Its companion paper is CC BY-NC 4.0, and the inspected repository text did not expose an unambiguous separate map licence. The map and threat figures are therefore linked rather than silently bundled for unrestricted commercial reuse. This does not reduce their value as cited research evidence. [S06, S16]

section: Reading the maps and the evidence responsibly
text: The 1957 ECAFE report documents the early development-planning history of the basin; the 1977 USGS report preserves an important hydrogeological baseline. Their population figures, administrative names, development assumptions and water-quality statements must not be presented as current Cambodian conditions. [S07, S12]

section: Reading the maps and the evidence responsibly
text: The earlier website package, GDMR presentation and field workbook remain supporting local materials. This publication extends their subject matter; it does not replace them, certify raw data or imply institutional endorsement. English is the full research text. The Khmer title and overview are an editorial summary and should receive fluent Khmer scientific review before use as a formal translation.
